title: Twenty-Four Indian Sailors Were on a Tanker Hit by a Suspected US Missile Off Oman. Two Are Missing.
excerpt: The Settebello, operated by an India-based company, was struck 20 nautical miles off Sohar. The Omani Navy responded to the distress call.
body:
Twenty-four of the twenty-eight sailors aboard a tanker struck by a suspected U.S. missile off the coast of Oman on Wednesday are Indian nationals. Two crew members are missing and one is injured.

The Settebello, a Palau-flagged chemical and oil products tanker, reported an engine room fire approximately 20 nautical miles northeast of Oman's port of Sohar, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency. British maritime security group Ambrey said the damage was "likely the result of U.S. operations to blockade Iranian ports."

A second maritime security source confirmed to Reuters that the vessel was likely hit by a U.S. missile. The Omani Navy responded to the ship's distress call.

India Scrambles for Answers

An Indian government source told Reuters that officials were urgently trying to establish whether the two missing crew members are among the Indian nationals aboard. The ship's India-based operator, listed in maritime databases, could not be reached for comment.

The vessel was partially laden and had last been located off Oman's coast on June 1, according to the MarineTraffic ship-tracking platform. Vanguard, a British maritime risk management group, identified the vessel and noted the Omani Navy's response.

U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the incident.

Ambrey noted that in past enforcement actions, "crews have been warned to gather on the bow of a vessel before an attack on the stern" — a protocol designed to minimise casualties. Whether such a warning was issued to the Settebello's crew remains unclear.

The Blockade's Human Cost

The United States began its blockade of Iran-related shipping on April 13, after Tehran severely curtailed traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — a chokepoint that before the war carried a fifth of the world's crude oil and liquefied natural gas. As of June 8, U.S. Central Command said its forces had disabled seven non-compliant vessels, redirected 134 others, and allowed 42 humanitarian aid vessels to pass.

Until Wednesday, there had been no reports of fatalities stemming from these enforcement operations. The Settebello incident changes that calculus. If any of the missing crew members are confirmed dead, it would mark the first known loss of life from U.S. blockade operations — and the victims would almost certainly be Indian.

India's merchant marine is among the world's largest. Indian seafarers crew a significant share of the global tanker fleet, and the waters around the Strait of Hormuz have become one of the most dangerous maritime zones on the planet since the war began in February.

A Broader Pattern of Vulnerability

The Settebello strike comes on the same day that Iran launched missile and drone attacks on U.S. bases in Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain — a retaliatory escalation after American strikes on Iranian air defences, ground control stations and radar sites near the Strait of Hormuz. Nearly all Iranian projectiles were intercepted, with no immediate U.S. casualties reported.

But the civilian toll is mounting in ways that rarely make headlines. India's external affairs ministry has issued sweeping travel advisories for the entire Middle East, urging Indian nationals to exercise extreme caution. In some high-risk zones, the directive has shifted from "avoid non-essential travel" to an explicit call for Indian citizens to leave.

An estimated 8 million Indians live and work in the Gulf states. They remit tens of billions of dollars annually — a lifeline for families back home and a structural pillar of India's current account. The war's disruption of shipping lanes, airspace closures and escalating military exchanges threaten not just their safety but the economic architecture that connects India to its diaspora.

What Comes Next

India's immediate priority is locating the two missing crew members. Diplomatic channels between New Delhi and Muscat are active, with the Indian embassy in Oman coordinating with the Omani Navy and local maritime authorities.

The broader question — how Indian seafarers caught between American enforcement operations and Iranian retaliation can be protected — has no easy answer. The Settebello was not an Iranian vessel. Its crew were not combatants. They were working men from India, doing one of the most dangerous jobs in the world, in waters that have become a warzone.

Their families are waiting for news.
